qs.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease?
o: Rheumatic heart disease is a long-term cardiac complication of acute rheumatic fever.
Rheumatic fever is caused by direct bacterial invasion of the heart valves.
Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease represent the exact same acute phase.
Rheumatic heart disease occurs concurrently during the initial pharyngitis episode.
qs.e: Rheumatic heart disease is the late manifestation and long-term consequence of acute rheumatic fever. The acute episode involves inflammation, whereas RHD results from chronic valve damage.

qs.q: What is the primary pathogenic mechanism responsible for tissue injury in acute rheumatic fever?
o: Direct toxic destruction by circulating streptococcal exotoxins in the myocardium
Immune-mediated delayed response causing cross-reactivity with host cardiac antigens
Suppurative bacterial colonization directly inside the endocardial valve leaflets
Granulomatous reaction driven by chronic fungal proliferation within connective tissues
qs.e: ARF is triggered by an immune-mediated delayed response where antibodies against group A streptococci cross-react with cardiac myosin and sarcolemmal proteins. This immune reaction causes inflammation rather than direct bacterial infection of the heart.

qs.q: Why do only about 25% of patients with acute rheumatic fever have a positive throat culture for group A streptococcus at the time of diagnosis?
o: There is a latent period of 2 to 4 weeks between the initial infection and the presentation of symptoms.
Group A streptococcus bacteria are completely eradicated by host immunity within minutes.
Throat cultures lack sensitivity due to rapid bacterial mutation in the bloodstream.
Patients usually seek medical attention during the acute pharyngitis phase before symptoms resolve.
qs.e: A latent period of 2 to 4 weeks occurs between the throat infection and the immune-mediated presentation of ARF, meaning the bacteria are often gone by the time symptoms appear. Serological tests like ASO titers are therefore more helpful at diagnosis.

qs.q: Under what clinical scenario can a presumptive diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever be made without evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection?
o: Isolated chorea or pancarditis, after excluding other causes
Migratory polyarthritis affecting large joints in a child
A patient presenting with simple erythema marginatum and fever
Recurrent episodes of arthralgia and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
qs.e: A presumptive diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever can be made without prior evidence of streptococcal infection specifically in cases of isolated chorea or pancarditis, provided other causes are excluded. This exception accounts for the long latency of certain manifestations.

qs.q: In a moderate or high-risk population, which of the following has been included as a major criterion for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever?
o: Aseptic monoarthritis
Isolated mild fever alone
Mild leukocytosis
Elevated blood urea nitrogen
qs.e: In moderate or high-risk populations, aseptic monoarthritis and polyarthralgia have been recognized as major manifestations for diagnosis. This contrasts with low-risk populations where traditional polyarthritis remains the standard major joint criterion.

qs.q: What is the baseline traditional requirement to establish a firm diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever according to the Jones criteria?
o: Two major manifestations or one major and two minor manifestations, plus evidence of recent streptococcal infection
Three minor manifestations and a confirmed positive throat culture for group A streptococcus
Only one major manifestation without any need for supportive serological evidence
Four minor manifestations combined with clinical signs of chronic valve failure
qs.e: A firm diagnosis requires two major manifestations or one major and two minor manifestations, along with evidence of a recent streptococcal infection. This ensures high diagnostic specificity to prevent over- or under-treatment.

qs.q: How is a low-risk population defined regarding the incidence of acute rheumatic fever in school-age children?
o: An incidence of less than 2 per 100,000 school-age children per year
An incidence of more than 10 per 100,000 school-age children per year
An incidence of exactly 19 per 100,000 school-age children per year
An overall regional incidence of 50 per 100,000 children
qs.e: Low-risk populations are specifically defined as those with an ARF incidence of less than 2 per 100,000 school-age children or a rheumatic heart disease all-age prevalence of less than 1 per 1,000 per year.

qs.q: What epidemiological pattern is most characteristic of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease globally?
o: It is primarily a disease of poverty and low socioeconomic status due to barriers in seeking medical care for pharyngitis.
It has the highest incidence rates in wealthy urban centers of North America and Western Europe.
It predominantly affects elderly populations older than 65 years with comorbid metabolic syndrome.
It shows an equal distribution across all global regions regardless of household crowding or hygiene.
qs.e: RHD is strongly linked to poverty and low socioeconomic status, where patients often do not seek medical attention when they contract pharyngitis. Developed nations have seen a sharp decline due to improved hygiene and reduced household crowding.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rheumatic fever is an autoimmune inflammation of the heart, joints, skin, and nervous system that follows untreated Group A streptococcal throat infection, mainly in children. Prompt recognition using the Jones criteria and secondary prophylaxis prevent permanent heart damage.

sections.p: Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is a post‑streptococcal immune reaction causing multi‑system inflammation. Diagnosis relies on the Jones criteria, which combine major and minor clinical findings with evidence of recent streptococcal infection.
b: Major: migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Minor: fever, arthralgia, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval.

t.b: Does the patient have recent streptococcal exposure? High titres support recent infection.

t.a: Throat culture or rapid antigen test
t.b: Is there a current streptococcal throat infection? Positive test confirms active infection; negative does not rule out prior infection.

sections.p: Severity is graded by cardiac involvement: mild (isolated valvulitis), moderate (murmur with heart failure signs), severe (heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or severe valvular regurgitation). Neurologic chorea is staged by functional impact.
b: Mild: no heart failure, normal ventricular function.
Moderate: mild heart failure, NYHA I‑II.
Severe: overt heart failure, NYHA III‑IV, or severe valve disease.

sections.p: The trigger is a recent Group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis, especially in settings with limited access to antibiotics. Other infections are rarely implicated.
b: Group A Streptococcus pharyngitis (most common).
Concurrent skin infection with GAS (rare).
In low‑resource settings, poor treatment adherence and crowded living conditions increase risk.

sections.p: Patients, usually 5‑15 years old, develop fever, migratory polyarthritis, and a new heart murmur. Skin findings (erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) and neurologic chorea may appear days to weeks after the sore throat.
b: Migratory arthritis affecting large joints, resolves within weeks.
Carditis: new regurgitant murmur, pericardial rub, or heart failure.
Sydenham chorea: involuntary movements, emotional lability.

sections.p: Investigations confirm recent streptococcal infection, assess cardiac involvement, and rule out mimics.
b: ECG for PR prolongation, arrhythmias.
Echocardiography to detect valvulitis, regurgitation, or pericardial effusion.

t.b: Is there evidence of carditis? PR prolongation or arrhythmia suggests myocardial involvement.
What is the extent of valvular damage? Detects regurgitation, thickening, or reduced function.
Are inflammatory markers elevated? Supports active inflammation; normal does not exclude ARF.

sections.p: Uncontrolled carditis can rapidly progress to heart failure, severe mitral or aortic regurgitation, and permanent rheumatic heart disease.
b: Sudden dyspnea, pulmonary edema, or hypotension.
New or worsening murmur with signs of heart failure.
Severe chorea causing injury or inability to care for self.

sections.p: Treat the underlying infection, suppress inflammation, and protect the heart. Use anti‑inflammatory agents and secondary prophylaxis to prevent recurrence.
b: Penicillin (or amoxicillin) for 10 days to eradicate GAS; chosen for narrow spectrum and safety.
Aspirin (high‑dose) for anti‑inflammatory effect; avoids steroids unless severe carditis.
Corticosteroids for severe carditis or refractory inflammation; avoid if mild disease.
Heart failure therapy (diuretics, ACE‑inhibitors) when indicated.

sections.p: Long‑term secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine penicillin G prevents recurrence and progression to rheumatic heart disease. Follow cardiac status with periodic echocardiography.
b: Monthly benzathine penicillin G for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer.
Echocardiogram at 6 months, then yearly if valve disease persists.
Educate families about early treatment of sore throat.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic ARF include septic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, viral myocarditis, and systemic lupus erythematosus.
b: Septic arthritis: usually single joint, high fever, positive joint fluid culture.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: chronic, not linked to recent strep.
Viral myocarditis: lacks migratory arthritis and streptococcal evidence.

sections.p: Normal ASO titres can occur if the infection was > 8 weeks ago or if the patient is a poor antibody responder; a negative throat culture does not exclude prior infection.
b: ASO may be low in early infection; repeat testing after 2 weeks if suspicion remains.
CRP/ESR can be modestly raised in other inflammatory conditions.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain
Rapidly worsening heart murmur with signs of heart failure
Severe chorea causing injury or inability to eat

faq.q: Why does a throat infection cause heart damage?
faq.a: Molecular mimicry makes antibodies against streptococcal antigens cross‑react with cardiac tissue, leading to inflammation.
No; only the streptococcal infection is contagious, not the autoimmune reaction.
It is rare but can occur, especially in those with untreated strep infections or poor access to care.

exam: List the major and minor Jones criteria and explain how they are applied.
Describe the pathophysiology linking Group A streptococcal infection to cardiac involvement.
Outline the acute management of severe carditis in rheumatic fever.
